defs: Probiotics
live microorganisms which when administered in adequate amounts confer a health benefit on the host
Living microbes that, in a big enough dose, have been shown to help you.
Prebiotics
a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit
Food for your helpful gut microbes — mostly certain fibers — that has a shown health benefit.
Postbiotics
preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host
Non-living (inactivated) microbes or their parts that still have a shown benefit.
Synbiotics
a mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit on the host
Live microbes plus their food, together in one product.
Fermented foods
foods made through desired microbial growth and enzymatic conversions of food components
Foods made by letting microbes work on them. Not all of them still contain live microbes.
live: Fermented foods, such as leavened breads, are baked after fermentation, effectively killing the fermentation microorganisms.

Some fermented foods are heated (baked, pasteurized, or made shelf-stable) after fermenting, which kills the microbes. Look for “live and active cultures” or a refrigerated, unpasteurized product if live microbes are what you want.
strain: if a specific kind of Lactobacillus helps prevent an illness, that doesn’t necessarily mean that another kind of Lactobacillus or any of the Bifidobacterium probiotics would do the same thing.
Evidence is strain-specific: results for one strain don’t carry over to others, even in the same family.
ev: In symptomatic children and adults with irritable bowel syndrome, we recommend the use of probiotics only in the context of a clinical trial.

The main U.S. gut-doctors’ guideline (AGA, 2020) says that for IBS, Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis and C. difficile infection, probiotics belong in research studies, not routine treatment. It suggested specific strains only for a few uses (such as preventing C. difficile while on antibiotics, pouchitis, and preterm infants in hospital).
in most instances, we still don’t know which probiotics are helpful and which are not.
There’s a lot of research, but for most uses it isn’t clear which products help, at what dose, or for whom.
the high-fermented-food diet steadily increased microbiota diversity and decreased inflammatory markers.

In one 17-week randomized diet study in healthy adults (18 per group), the high-fermented-food diet raised gut-microbe variety and lowered some inflammation markers. It’s one small study — promising, not proof.
safe: The risk of harmful effects from probiotics is greater in people with severe illnesses or compromised immune systems.
If you are immunocompromised or seriously ill, talk with your care team before taking probiotic supplements.
Cases of severe or fatal infections have been reported in premature infants who were given probiotics
Premature babies should not be given probiotics except under their medical team’s care.
Eating a large amount of fiber in a short period of time can cause intestinal gas (flatulence), bloating, and abdominal cramps.
Adding fiber or prebiotic foods quickly can cause gas and bloating. Increase slowly over a few weeks and drink fluids.
abx: We did not find a source in our citation set that sets a specific spacing between antibiotics and probiotics, so the app gives no timing advice — ask your pharmacist.
